title: StreamConductor: length-adaptive slot allocator for mixed prompt/response workloads
creator: Aidan Chen
description:
Problem: Our continuous batching scheduler performs well for homogeneous sequence lengths but degrades on mixed prompt/response workloads where short prompts often interleave with very long generation responses. This causes KV cache churn, GPU memory fragmentation, and increased tail latency for short interactive requests.

Goal: Implement and tune a length-adaptive slot allocator (StreamConductor) that: (1) soft-reserves slots for short-turn streams, (2) adapts slot tenure based on observed response lengths and KV residency, and (3) coordinates with KV prefetching and GPU slab compaction to reduce fragmentation without sacrificing throughput.

Success criteria: measurable reduction in P99 latency for short-turn sessions by >=25% under mixed workloads, overall token throughput drop <=3%, and GPU memory fragmentation index reduced by 20% on average during 1h traffic bursts.

Scope: design allocator heuristics, integrate with continuous-batcher core, extend KV cache eviction hooks to expose residency signals, add GPU slab defrag trigger, run controlled experiments, and roll out as an opt-in runtime flag before enabling by default.
acceptance_criteria: P99 latency for short-turn (<=8 token prompt, <=16 token response) flows reduced by >=25% in benchmark mix A
End-to-end throughput (tokens/sec) change <= -3% compared to baseline under benchmark mix B
GPU fragmentation metric (slab fragmentation ratio) improved by >=20% during 60-minute burst test
No regression in correctness or KV lookup hit rate (<2% change)
Feature gated behind runtime flag stream_conductor.enabled and integrates with existing canary rollout tooling
experiments: Experiment 1 (local perf rig): baseline continuous-batcher vs StreamConductor prototype with 3 soft-reserve levels. Results: short-turn P99 improved ~18%, throughput -1.8%, fragmentation -9%. (logs in perf rig: https://dash.redwood.local/perf/exp-2026-03-07)

Experiment 2 (staging, 4 hours): tuned slot-tenure hysteresis + KV-residency signal. Results: short-turn P99 improved 27%, throughput -2.7%, fragmentation -22%. Observed occasional misassignments when two long responses started concurrently in the same slab.
Planned Experiment 3 (canary on 5% production traffic): evaluate real-world traffic patterns and verify fallback behavior under GPU pressure (target start 2026-03-18)
Key metrics collected: per-stream slot-age histogram, KV residency ratio, slab fragmentation ratio, token throughput, end-to-end tail latencies
design_decisions: Use a soft-reserve mechanism instead of strict partitioning to avoid unused capacity during high long-response load
Expose KV residency as a first-class signal (kv_residency_score 0..1) from the cache so allocator can prefer streams with hot KVs
Introduce slot-tenure hysteresis: extend tenure for streams that demonstrate rising length mid-session to reduce eviction churn
Trigger GPU slab compaction when fragmentation ratio > 0.35 and predicted near-term long-response probability > 0.6
Integrate with existing continuous-batcher admission controller and keep scheduler API backwards-compatible
implementation_tasks: Allocator core: implement StreamConductor module with per-stream window tracking and soft-reserve logic (ENG work)
KV cache: add kv_residency_score export and a lightweight subscription API for allocator to receive updates
GPU runtime: add slab fragmentation metrics and compaction trigger endpoint
Metrics: add dashboards for per-stream slot-age, kv_residency, slab-frag, and allele of P50/P95/P99 by prompt/response class
Testing: unit tests for tenure hysteresis, integration tests on perf rig, and staging canary harness
Docs: runtime flag docs + migration notes for Dedicated and Private deployments
rollout_plan: Step 0: Merge feature behind stream_conductor.enabled=false by default (PR link below)
Step 1: Deploy to perf-rig and run benchmark mixes (automated) -> validate acceptance criteria
Step 2: Canary on 5% of production traffic for 72 hours, monitor: P99 short-turn, slab-frag, token throughput
Step 3: If stable, increase canary to 25% for 24 hours and run chaos tests (GPU eviction/failover)
Step 4: On success, flip default to enabled for Runtime-2.4 with a one-week revert window
risks: Over-reserving can starve long-running generation workloads and reduce throughput; mitigated by soft-reserve and adaptive thresholds
Incorrect KV residency signals may bias allocation and increase misses; add statistical smoothing and fallback to LRU if signals are noisy
GPU compaction is expensive; compaction triggers must be conservative and rate-limited to avoid disrupting serving
Interplay with quantized models: different memory layouts may affect fragmentation; include model-type in slab heuristics
